entries.title: White Sox outfielder Everson Pereira says he won't think twice about running into walls
entries.summary: <p>Everson Pereira hasn’t played for the White Sox since June 17, when he left a game at Yankee Stadium after crashing into the center-field wall while making an incredible catch. Though he suffered a concussion and missed more than five weeks, he said he won’t change how he plays.</p><p>“I’m going to try to catch the ball no matter what,” Pereira said.</p><p>The Sox put that to the test quickly, starting Pereira in center field against the Yankees on Monday after activating him from the injured list. They optioned outfielder Junior Perez to Triple-A Charlotte.</p><p>“He’s 100% ready to play, or else he wouldn’t be here,” manager Will Venable said.</p><p>Pereira is returning from his third stint on the IL this season after missing time with a sprained left ankle and a strained right pectoral. He hit only .160 on a seven-game rehab assignment at Charlotte, but he capped it off with a home run Sunday.</p><p>Venable said the right-handed-hitting Pereira will face left-handed pitchers more to start but eventually could see some righties. Venable said Pereira brings “a ton of power,” though it has yet to manifest itself consistently in the majors. In 71 career games entering Monday, he has five home runs, including three in 21 games with the Sox this season.</p><p>Pereira, who suffered the first concussion of his career, said he began feeling fully like himself again last week. The recovery process wasn’t easy.</p><p>“I was feeling good like two weeks ago, but I was worried I couldn’t pass the reaction test,” he said through a translator. “If I couldn’t pass, I couldn’t be active. It was different from a regular injury because the treatment is different. There’s all different things like stuff you have to remember, and you have to give quick answers to different questions. It’s very difficult.”</p><p>The Sox acquired Pereira in a trade with the Rays in November, and his first season admittedly has been frustrating even beyond the injuries. His on-base percentage was only .299.</p><p>“But there’s nothing I can do about it,” he said. “Thank God I’m here right now, and hopefully I can stay healthy for the rest of the season.”</p><h3>Colson at DH</h3><p>Shortstop Colson Montgomery filled the DH spot in the Sox’ lineup to get him off his feet because of a bruised right shin he keeps fouling balls off. He sat out of the Sox’ 12-3 victory Sunday against the Astros.</p><p>“Thought it made sense,” Venable said. “I think he could’ve played short today but just want to give him a little more recovery. It will be day-to-day. Likely playing shortstop [Tuesday].”</p><p>This would be Montgomery’s first full major-league season, and Venable wants to be careful when he can be.</p><p>“I think for all of our players, navigating a full season is something we have to be mindful of,” he said. “Whether that means off days or DH days, it’s something we got to work with the player to make sure we can get to the end and do it performing at a high level and healthy.”</p><h3>Hays building up</h3><p>Outfielder Austin Hays continues to work his way back from a strained left calf that has him on the 60-day injured list. Hays, whom the Sox signed to a one-year, $6 million contract in February, has played in only 12 games this season. He also was on the IL in April with a strained right hamstring.</p><p>In the first seven games of his rehab assignment at Charlotte, Hays is slugging .560 with two homers, including one Sunday.</p><p>“Still in a spot where he’s continuing to build volume and make sure that he’s recovering well,” Venable said. “Obviously, the homer’s nice to see, but still building up there. I think he’s been up to seven innings out in the field mixed in with some DH spots. So as he gets more and more innings, making sure that he’s recovering well afterward is a big part of building his volume.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Rookie Noah Schultz doesn't help his case to stay in White Sox' rotation
entries.summary: <p>Perhaps Noah Schultz knew he was pitching for his spot in the White Sox’ rotation when he took the mound Monday against the Yankees. He struck out the side in the first inning, his only blemish being a double to future Hall of Famer Paul Goldschmidt. No shame in that.</p><p>The rookie left-hander needed a strong showing after allowing five runs in 3 ⅔ innings in his last start. Though he didn’t walk anyone — a bugaboo for most of his season — he surrendered 11 hits. Filling the strike zone is one thing. Having those pitches come back at you is another.</p><p>“The strikes are something that was on top of the list, to get him in the zone with his stuff being so good,” manager Will Venable said before the game. “And he was able to do that. But then there’s some shapes that he’s trying to get back, too, whether that’s more depth on the sweeper, more [vertical] fastball. Also, of course, maintaining the ability to attack the zone and maintain count leverage.”</p><p>But Schultz couldn’t stay on track. Fantastic catches by right fielder Braden Montgomery and left fielder Randal Grichuk on three hard-hit balls kept Schultz out of trouble in the second and third innings. He fell apart in the fourth, allowing two walks and a single before Venable pulled him, perhaps for the last time this season.</p><p>Venable disputed the game’s importance for Schultz personally — “It’s an important outing because we have to find a way to beat the Yankees” — but there’s no escaping this pitching predicament: The Sox can’t afford to develop a pitcher while pursuing a playoff spot. And they certainly can’t afford their starters hitting the showers early too often.</p><p>In their last 23 games, only right-hander Sean Burke has thrown at least six innings, which he has done four times. Schultz has been the only one in the rotation unable to get past five innings in that span, and he lasted just 3 ⅓ innings Monday.</p><p>For the Sox to hang on to their lead in the American League Central, they’ll need more length from their rotation. General manager Chris Getz figures to seek help for the stretch run by the trade deadline next Monday, and he might’ve begun his shopping in the bargain basement.</p><p>On Sunday, the Sox acquired right-hander Jose Urquidy from the Pirates for a low-level minor-league pitcher. It was far from a blockbuster, but it might portend how Getz tries to bolster the pitching staff.</p><p>Urquidy’s best season was in 2022, when he went 13-8 with a 3.94 ERA in 29 games (28 starts) for the Astros, who went on to win the World Series. He has pitched in 15 postseason games in his career. The Sox’ starters have combined for zero postseason starts.</p><p>This isn’t to say Urquidy will be a savior. He hasn’t pitched in the majors since April 13. After signing with the Pirates in February, Urquidy posted an 8.53 ERA in 6⅓ innings of relief, prompting his demotion to Triple-A. At Indianapolis, he had a 3.66 ERA in 17 starts (83 innings).</p><p>But if the Sox need to make a move, Venable said Urquidy will be ready and waiting at Charlotte.</p><p>“He’s an option for us,” Venable said. “We know how quickly things change here. There’ll be a need. It could be tomorrow, for all we know. Whatever the need is, I think that there’s versatility there with him. I know he’s got the ability to pitch in bulk but also come out of the pen and give us different looks. He’s a piece that we’re excited to have.”</p><p>With the starters consistently failing to go deep into games, Urquidy probably won’t be enough, or even a solution, for that matter. But in his short time as GM, Getz has shown he can find quality pitching at bargain prices. He’ll need to do just that if the organization decides Schultz needs time at Charlotte to get himself together.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Temporary protected status ends for Haitian and Syrian immigrants
entries.summary: <p>Temporary protected status ended Monday for more than 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians, leaving them vulnerable to being deported to the countries they fled — countries still coping with violence and instability.</p><p>In June, the Supreme Court allowed the administration of President Donald Trump to end the 36-year-old Temporary Protected Status program for hundreds of thousands of Haitian and Syrian migrants.</p><p>“People are feeling like this country has let them down too,” said Patrick Brutus, vice president and co-founder of the Haitian American Professional Network. “They’ve had to watch their country tumble into destabilization from afar, and now families may have to face leaving their children behind or taking children to a dangerous place they’ve never been.”</p><p>In a statement, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said TPS had been used as a "de facto amnesty program" for "too long."</p><p>It was created by Congress in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife. The protections are available only to people who have been continuously present in the U.S. since the date of designation, and DHS can extend it in increments of up to 18 months.</p><p>Haitians were first granted TPS in 2010 after a 7.0 magnitude earthquake killed hundreds of thousands, with extensions granted as <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/haiti-violence-gangs-port-au-prince-431b915e4143adddfacb105473ee604d" target="_blank" >gang violence continues to displace more than a million people</a> after the assassination of the country's president in 2021.</p><p>Syrians were first granted TPS in 2012 during a civil war that lasted decades until the fall of the national government in late 2024. Ongoing <a class="Link" href="https://www.cfr.org/global-conflict-tracker/conflict/conflict-syria#TransitionUnderAhmedalSharaa2024Present-2" target="_blank" ><u>fighting and persecution of minorities</u></a> has led to thousands more deaths since.</p><p>The Trump administration has argued the immigrants were poorly vetted and that DHS, not judges, had sole authority to end the protections. They also argued the countries people have been granted TPS from <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/RS20844#_Toc207985226" target="_blank" ><u>are safe</u></a>, though the U.S. Department of State urges Americans not to travel to both <a class="Link" href="https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/international-travel/International-Travel-Country-Information-Pages/Haiti.html?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=44031958015&gbraid=0AAAAAqbBk5uW_lXcTNQj_81sWIY4YrIVQ&gclid=Cj0KCQjwg5zTBhCLARIsAP2AFU5oDFTKu6mwrW80sJpcBX9fPAOyj0Q3W8TYTTpyHXCZIhL-2iuSd2kaAuzyEALw_wcB" target="_blank" ><u>Haiti</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://travel.state.gov/en/international-travel/travel-advisories/syria.html?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=44031958015&gbraid=0AAAAAqbBk5uW_lXcTNQj_81sWIY4YrIVQ&gclid=Cj0KCQjwg5zTBhCLARIsAP2AFU5vaq1KRYiA6252HHYP51kajdLucW1-g7sLcaDiTQzHReFq_Xg5ke0aArQPEALw_wcB" target="_blank" ><u>Syria</u></a> due to ongoing dangers there.</p><p>Even still, the U.S. Supreme Court’s 6-3 conservative majority agreed with the Trump administration, allowing it to end protections for Haitians and Syrians. The court <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/05/19/supreme-court-allows-trump-to-strip-protections-from-some-venezuelans-deportations-could-follow" target="_blank" ><u>allowed TPS for 350,000 immigrants</u></a> from Venezuela and thousands more from other countries to be terminated in a separate decision last year.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/24/chaotic-crowded-chicago-immigration-mega-court-hearings-are-fueling-record-deportation-orders" >Chaotic, crowded Chicago immigration mega court hearings are fueling record deportation orders</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/22/mexico-seeks-accountability-in-chicago-area-ice-death-and-16-others-can-it-force-the-u-s-to-act" >Mexico seeks accountability in Chicago-area ICE death and 16 others. Can it force the U.S. to act?</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/10/asylum-russia-ukraine-war-tiulenev-immigration" >A dissident family fled Russia after their home was set on fire. Trump’s administration wants to deport them.</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Elsie Hernandez, founder of the Haitian American Museum of Chicago and a nurse who was on the ground in the aftermath of the 2010 earthquake, said things have only gotten worse in Haiti.</p><p>“You have people who have built their lives [in the U.S.], bought houses, opened businesses, and sent their kids to school,” Hernandez said. “It’s 16 years of a build-up of life, to have it all destroyed. … Temporary would mean the conditions they left have improved, but it hasn’t. It’s gotten worse.”</p><p>Immigrant advocates recommend those who had TPS get legal guidance as soon as possible, and for those who need to, trying to find legal guardians for their children and avenues to protect assets like homes and other property.</p><p>Lawrence Benito, executive director of the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, said immigrant groups are preparing for an enforcement surge from ICE, and that the strategy for advocacy organizations to protect former TPS holders now is the same as other U.S. residents without legal status.</p><div class="Enhancement" Some may still qualify for asylum or other routes to avoid losing legal status, such as if they have a family or work sponsor.</p><p>However, federal agents have increasingly targeted people at courthouses, which could both keep people away and mean they are detained before having the chance to seek other means of protection.</p><p>“If the past is any indicator, this is an opportunity for them to expand their operations, and we’re on alert,” Benito said.</p><p>Brutus worries the nearly million people from 17 other countries also on temporary protected status — including hundreds of thousands from Venezuela, El Salvador and Ukraine — could face the same.</p><p>“This is just a first test,” Brutus said. “My recommendation to others here under TPS, or any other similar condition, start to get ready with understanding your legal options and organize to put public policy on your side. … I’m hopeful Chicagoans will protect their own.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Associated Press</i></p>

entries.title: Swinging hot bat, reserve infielder Pedro Ramirez impressing Cubs with work in limited playing time
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS — The <b>Pedro Ramirez</b> Experience has been a good one for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a>.</p><p>The young infielder has impressed team brass in his first taste of the big leagues this season, settling nicely into a reserve role.</p><p>Ramirez, who was among the Cubs’ highest-rated prospects when the season began, has managed to stay effective while not playing every day.</p><p>Entering play Monday, he had a seven-game hit streak during which he was batting .440 and had four multihit performances.</p><p>‘‘He’s really handled a lot of these situations really well, like not playing every day, still being productive,’’ manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said last week. ‘‘And defensively he’s been really good, as well, especially at third base. He’s been excellent. There’s a lot to like.</p><p>‘‘For a 22-year-old to come up and play sporadically and be on the bench and still be a contributor, it’s been fun to watch.’’</p><p>Limited playing time sometimes can work against a player, and the Cubs have stated their intent to cycle through youngsters such as outfielder <b>Kevin Alcantara</b>, infielder <b>James Triantos</b> and catcher/designated hitter <b>Moises Ballesteros</b> with a different roster spot. Turns in the majors have included — and figure to continue to include — going back down to keep from rusting on the bench.</p><p>Ramirez hasn’t rusted, however. He brought a .305 batting average into the game Monday, with an OPS-plus of 122. That means he has been 22% more productive than the average major-league hitter, a group that includes a lot of guys with much more big-league experience.</p><p>As the Cubs chart their future — and president <b>Jed Hoyer</b> goes to work ahead of the trade deadline, with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/24/cubs-trade-rumors-mlb-trade-deadline-top-prospects-james-triantos-pedro-ramirez-matt-shaw-jed-hoyer" target="_blank" >young players part of the equation</a> — Ramirez has made a mighty positive first impression.</p><p>‘‘We’ve talked about not playing,’’ Counsell said. ‘‘[Before the All-Star break] in Cincinnati, we were in a stretch where he wasn’t playing that much. . . . It’s the first time it’s ever happened to him. For guys like Pedro — you’re 22, you’re in the big leagues already — you have never not come to the field and [wondered whether] you’re in the lineup. You play every day.</p><p>‘‘We had a good conversation about that. But he understands all that. He’s got a really good frame of reference for it. His work on those types of things has been the right kind of work. He’s just kind of ahead of it. He’s ahead of how you approach situations, and that’s really impressive.’’</p><h3>Cabrera’s comeback</h3><p>Right-hander <b>Edward Cabrera</b> is nearing a minor-league rehab assignment on his way back from a strained hamstring that has kept him out for a month.</p><p>Cabrera will pitch Friday for Triple-A Iowa in the first of three planned rehab outings. Should all go well, he figures to return to the rotation in the middle of August.</p><p>While getting Cabrera back will be a big deal for a pitching staff still dealing with the effects of an avalanche of injuries, he has yet to deliver the type of results the Cubs hoped he would when they acquired him in an offseason trade with the Marlins. He has a 5.10 ERA in 14 starts.</p><h3>Rhymes with ‘pants’</h3><p>The Cubs called up reliever <b>Andrew Wantz</b> from Iowa after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/27/cubs-jameson-taillon-dfa-mlb-trade-deadline-pitching-jed-hoyer-craig-counsell-rotation" target="_blank" >designating veteran righty <b>Jameson Taillon</b> for assignment</a>.</p><p>Wantz joined the Cubs at the start of June after he was let go by the Rays. He had some good seasons with the Angels, posting a 3.85 ERA in three seasons (2021-23).</p><p>He had a 4.32 ERA in 25 innings spanning seven outings for Iowa.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" entries.title: Many Americans are paying for data centers. They shouldn't have to.
entries.summary: <p>Pull up your electric bill. Somewhere in that number, you are paying for a building you will never enter.</p><p>Data centers are going up everywhere. They need enormous amounts of electricity. Somebody must pay to connect them and build the plants and lines they need.</p><p>In state after state, that somebody is you.</p><p>Not everywhere. Texas requires the largest new power users to pay more of their connection costs and cut demand when the grid is strained. The data centers came anyway.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-270000" name="module-270000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Ohio now makes large new customers pay for much of the electricity they reserve, whether they use it or not. Projections for new demand then fell sharply. Much of the emergency was companies holding space they might never fill.</p><p>Virginia chose differently. It gives data centers a tax break on their equipment. Good Jobs First estimates that subsidy cost Virginia schools $267 million in one year.</p><p>Illinois lawmakers let a similar bill die without a vote.</p><p>Neither list sorts cleanly by party. Before you file this as a new problem, meet my great-great-grandfather. Edward David Bland was born into slavery in Dinwiddie County, Virginia, in 1848. Thirty-one years later, he was helping write that state’s laws.</p><p>He served three terms in the House of Delegates and sat on the Committee on Schools and Colleges. That was not a coincidence. That was the point.</p><p>Virginia was fighting over debt borrowed before the Civil War for canals and railroads. With interest, it had passed $45 million.</p><p>One side said pay every penny, whatever it took. They were called the Funders.</p><p>Here is what it was taking.</p><p>Virginia was starving its public schools to pay bondholders. The bondholders lived in New York and London. The children lived in Petersburg and Danville.</p><p>The other side said the debt would be paid but not out of the schoolhouse. They were the Readjusters. Black and white together. Farmers, freedmen and a former Confederate general named William Mahone.</p><p>A man born into slavery and a man who wore gray were counting the same votes on one floor. They ran Virginia for four years. In 1882, they cut the state’s share of the debt by roughly a third and refinanced the rest over 50 years.</p><p>Then they spent the difference. They put money back into public schools. They funded schools with Black teachers. They repealed the poll tax. They tore down the whipping post.</p><p>The Readjusters knew something we forgot. Whoever profits should not get to send the bill to whoever cannot say no.</p><p>I am not against data centers. This country cannot afford to fall behind in artificial intelligence, and the reasons are not all about money.</p><p>I am against making working families subsidize the world’s richest companies.</p><p>It does not always take a governor. A small town in Illinois capped a data center’s water use, with penalties if it went over.</p><p>A town council did that. Now let me tell you how the Readjusters lost. That is the part we forget.</p><p>They were not beaten on the debt. They won that argument. In October 1883, their opponents warned that Black residents of Danville had gained too much power. On Nov. 3, market day, a street fight became a shooting. Five men died. Four were Black.</p><p>For three days, armed white men walked the streets and kept Black Virginians from the polls. The election came that week. Democrats took both houses.</p><p>They never took the schools back. The new legislature left the school money alone. It left the whipping post gone. It left the debt settled.</p><p>They did not undo the policy. They undid the voters.</p><p>In 1902, a new state constitution stripped most Black Virginians of the ballot for more than 60 years. They were not defeated by a better plan. They were defeated by a campaign that made white farmers fear Black farmers more than the men taking money from both.</p><p>It is the cheapest trick in American politics, and it has never once been out of stock. The people paying for these deals live in Loudoun County and Memphis, in white towns in Iowa and Black neighborhoods in Atlanta, in union halls and farmhouses.</p><p>They are already paying the same bill. They just have not been asked to fight it together.</p><p>Somebody will work hard to make sure they never do.</p><p>My great-great-grandfather learned his letters at a night school for freedmen after the war. He was 17. Then he sat on the committee that funded schools so other children would not wait.</p><p>He knew exactly what a school was worth. Go find out what your state did.</p><p>Then find out who let it happen.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fe0000" name="module-fe0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Wife's dream trip wouldn't include her grumpy husband
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have just retired and want to spend the summer taking a long road trip from Florida to Alaska and back. I've dreamed about it all my life and finally have the time and money to do it.</p><p>My husband hates long road trips, and I don't want to take him. He would be miserable and make me miserable in the process. Further, he has a list of demands — no more than six hours of driving per day, a nice hotel every night rather than camping out, which I prefer, and leasing a gas-guzzling SUV rather than my energy-efficient midsized car — that would triple the amount of time and money this will cost. I suspect some or all of his demands are passive-aggressive because he really doesn't want the trip to happen.</p><p>I understand my husband not wanting to sit at home alone for six weeks while I enjoy myself photographing bears, moose and elk in the Yukon Territory, and I do worry about his ability to take care of himself and the house. Honestly, though, I'm not sure our marriage could survive this trip. I'm seriously considering just sneaking out the door and sending him postcards. Any ideas? — <i>SOLO TRAVELER</i></p><p><b>DEAR SOLO TRAVELER:</b> This is your dream trip. If you don't go, or if you let your husband spoil it with his demands and complaints, you will end up resenting him. You don't need to sneak out. Instead, leave detailed instructions on caring for the homestead, and arrange for a friend or family member to check in on him regularly while you're away. If you set him up for success, you won't come home to a pile of smoking rubble or a steaming husband.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been in cancer treatment for the past 10 years. I have infusions, monthly MRI and CT scans, six doctors and nine medications. No one other than my psychologist ever asks me how I am. I do look OK, so even my mother never asks. My sister overheard Mom ask my other sister to find out what I'm doing to my hair. My hair looks thicker because it became coarse due to the chemo.</p><p>I don't want to be a crybaby, but I would appreciate it if someone just acknowledged that I have cancer. When I once complained to my mom that I have to take too many drugs, her response was, "Well, you have money!" Do you have any suggestions? — <i>GLOSSED OVER</i></p><p><b>DEAR GLOSSED OVER:</b> Please allow me to offer my sympathy over your struggles with cancer. The reason your family doesn't bring it up may be because it makes them sad, and they worry that talking about it may upset you.</p><p>You have the right to press them on the matter. Tell your mom you need her support and would like to be able to talk about your health issues with her. If you wish to bring your sisters into the circle, talk to them all together. The more family you have in the loop, the stronger you will be for the remainder of your treatment.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>For an excellent guide to becoming a better conversationalist and a more sociable person, order "How to Be Popular." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds), to: Dear Abby, Popularity Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Chicago’s mayoral campaign revs up as circulation of nominating petitions starts
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson’s reelection petitions will hit the streets Tuesday — the first day to start gathering the 12,500 signatures needed to qualify for the mayoral ballot — but that doesn’t mean the embattled incumbent has decided to seek a second term.</p><p>Johnson’s political director Christian Perry said it simply means there are “groups that supported us last time that would like to see him run” and there is a “good deal of organic energy on the ground to see his leadership continue.”</p><p>“They reached out to us, asked if it was OK, and we gave the OK that they could absolutely” circulate petitions on Johnson’s behalf. “But the mayor still hadn’t come to a decision,” Perry said.</p><p>Until Johnson officially launches his campaign for a second term, there’s always a chance that he won’t — even though his political foot soldiers in the Chicago Teachers Union will have no trouble gathering more than enough signatures by the Oct. 26 filing deadline to get him on the ballot and keep him there.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/07/15/alexi-giannoulias-brandon-johnson-potential-mayoral-candidates-campaign-fundraising-gap" >With mayoral race looming, Mayor Johnson falls further behind Giannoulias in fundraising</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>That’s not the case with the rest of the crowded mayoral field.</p><p>Veteran political operative Victor Reyes, who has joined the mayoral campaign team of cardiologist Dr. Lisa Nee, said he expects the field of roughly a dozen mayoral challengers to shrink to eight candidates who can gather 25,000 valid signatures — the amount he believes is needed to survive a petition challenge.</p><p>“It’s going to be the institutional candidates who survive — the candidates who can afford to buy all of those signatures,” said Reyes, who ran the now-defunct Hispanic Democratic Organization at the center of the city hiring scandal under former Mayor Richard M. Daley.</p><p></p><p>Reyes said he has advised newcomer Nee’s campaign to budget $150,000 just to get on the ballot and stay on it.</p><p></p><p>“When I worked for Daley, we filed 100,000 [signatures]. The Daley operation would get 50,000 and the ward organizations would give us a whole bunch as well. Today, you don’t have ward organizations, and you don’t have patronage, so everybody’s got to pay vendors and contractors to get signatures,” Reyes said.</p><p>“You get a few volunteers, but nowhere near what you will get from professional organizations. And it’s expensive. You’ve got to pay vendors anywhere from $4 to $5 to $6 per signature. The closer you get to the end of the signature [deadline], it goes up. Then it’s $10 a signature, and it goes crazy because people are scrambling to get valid signatures.”</p><h3>When filing of nominating petitions begins</h3><p>The first day to file nominating petitions is Oct. 19. The last day is Oct. 26. The five-day objection period begins on Oct. 27 and ends on Nov. 2.</p><p>That triggers the painstaking, costly process of attorneys examining the signatures of rival candidates. Reyes calls that pivotal period “structuring the race.” </p><p>With a campaign war chest of nearly $22 million, Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias, who has not formally announced yet, can afford to challenge the nominating petitions of outgoing Illinois Comptroller <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/06/11/chicago-mayoral-challenger-susana-mendoza-pension-crisis-state-comptroller" >Susana Mendoza,</a> Cook County Board of Review Commissioner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/06/11/chicago-mayoral-challenger-susana-mendoza-pension-crisis-state-comptroller" >George Cardenas,</a> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/01/07/us-rep-mike-quigley-mayoral-run-2027-brandon-johnson" >U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley</a> or anyone else he thinks might siphon support from him.</p><p>Giannoulias might choose to try to knock off the ballot a few of the political newcomers if he thinks they could draw enough single-digit support to keep him out of a potential runoff, or prevent him from winning the 50%-plus-one needed to win the race outright in the first round.</p><div class="Enhancement" I’m not picking on him. I’m just saying it’s got to be somebody who can handle it," Pappas said.</p><p>The Giannoulias campaign declined to comment on Pappas' remark. </p><p></p><p></p><p>Giannoulias is already using the millions he has received from business leaders, along with support within trade unions, to blanket the airwaves with feel-good commercials that boost his name recognition.</p><p> Cardenas barely survived a petition challenge for his seat on the Cook County Board of Review. His mayoral nominating petitions will hit the streets Tuesday — this time with “controls in place” to make certain those signatures are “good from the get-go.”</p><p>“Last time, it was a district, and our folks did not do due diligence to verify that. A lot of our signatures turned out to be out of the district. We won’t have to worry about that this time. This is the city. They won’t be going to the 'burbs,” Cardenas said. “We’re walking on eggshells because of what happened last time. It won’t happen this time." </p><p>Johnson has just over $631,309 in the bank, $21 million less than Giannoulias. </p><p>The mayor's failure to shift his fundraising into high gear, his refusal to declare for reelection and his anemic public approval ratings have fueled speculation that Johnson may just walk away after a single term and avoid the political embarrassment that Lori Lightfoot suffered by becoming the first incumbent mayor in 40 years to be eliminated in the first round. </p><p>A strategy memo prepared by Michael Ruemmler and Jonathan Swain, top executives of One Future Illinois, a public policy nonprofit created for a more moderate mayoral and City Council agenda, outlines the rocky road ahead for Johnson. It points to a poll of 801 registered Chicago voters conducted for One Future Illinois June 9-15 that shows Johnson with a 66% percent disapproval rate and 71% “unlikely to vote for his re-election.”</p><p>“These are not the numbers of a mayor preparing to run on results. They point to a narrower strategy: Consolidate the remaining base, divide the opposition and exploit every advantage of incumbency,” the memo states.</p><p>Noting that Johnson is “cash-poor, but City Hall rich,” the memo predicts the embattled incumbent will “give every part of his remaining coalition a reason to fear his defeat.”</p><p>“Teachers will hear school-closings. But Perry said he is confident Johnson will have the resources he needs to win a second term.</p><p>"Paul Vallas lit almost $30 million on fire to not be successful," Perry said, referring to Johnson's opponent in the 2023 mayoral runoff.</p>

entries.title: Extreme heat blamed for 7 deaths in Cook County this year, the most in more than a decade
entries.summary: <p>David P. Sopys’ family grew worried after he missed their Fourth of July barbecue.</p><p>Sopys, 46, lived on and off at various facilities while living with a learning disability, but he always came home for the holidays, said Chamille Sopys, his niece.</p><p>“He always comes over for any holiday, especially when food’s involved,” Chamille Sopys said. “It was just kind of weird that he hadn’t called or said anything. [My mother] doesn’t go that many days without talking to him at all.”</p><p>A few days later, the family learned Sopys died July 1, days before the holiday. On Monday, autopsy results showed Sopys died from heat exposure combined with cocaine and two prescription medications, fluoxetine and aripiprazole. His niece says they believe fentanyl also contributed to his death.</p><p>It was the seventh heat-related death so far this year in Cook County. That marks the most people who have died from heat-related causes in a single year in more than a decade, according to a WBEZ analysis of data from the Cook County medical examiner’s office.</p><p>Sopys had been outside with a group of people around 6:30 p.m. on July 1, in the 6300 block of South Campbell Avenue in the Chicago Lawn neighborhood when he became unresponsive, according to Chicago police. He was taken to Little Company of Mary Hospital where he was later pronounced dead.</p><p>Chicago police said Monday that the investigation into his death remained pending.</p><p>His death means the heat this summer has caused more deaths than in 2022 and 2019 when the county logged six heat-related deaths in each of those years, according to the WBEZ analysis. This month is the deadliest month for heat-related causes since at least 2015, the most recent year for which data is readily available.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-c20000" name="html-embed-module-c20000"></a><div style="min-height:514px" id="datawrapper-vis-SEdUK"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/SEdUK/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-SEdUK"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/SEdUK/full.png" alt="Seven people have died from heat-related causes in Cook County, the most in one year since 2015 (Column Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>But other past heat waves have been attributed to more deaths.</p><p>Chicago’s deadliest heat wave happened in 1995 when more than 700 people died. Chicago also suffered <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/8/30/18354264/a-look-back-at-chicago-s-deadly-1995-heat-wave" target="_blank" ><u>deadly heat waves</u></a> in 1999, when 10 people died, and in 2012, when 22 people died.</p><p>Sopys is the fourth person in their 40s who died from heat-related causes this year. The other people whose deaths this year have been attributed to the heat are: Stephanie Rodriguez, 45; David Gonzalez, 44; Barbara Whigham, 71; Mike Rodriguez, 57; Daniel Machnikowski, 69; and Victor Ferguson, 48. One of the deaths occurred in north suburban Evanston. All of the other six deaths occurred in Chicago neighborhoods on the city’s South, Southwest or West sides.</p><p>On the day Sopys died, the temperature at O’Hare Airport reached 95 degrees, according to the National Weather Service. The Chicago area had been placed under an extreme heat warning when he died. Six of the deaths happened during the first four days of July. That’s the most heat-related deaths in a four-day span since at least 2015.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-0e0000" name="html-embed-module-0e0000"></a><div style="min-height:885px" id="datawrapper-vis-0lM9g"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/0lM9g/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-0lM9g"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/0lM9g/full.png" alt="Seven people have died due to heat-related causes in Cook County, mainly on Chicago's South Side (Locator map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Chamille Sopys said her mother had last talked to her uncle the morning of July 1. The family knew he had recently gotten out of a facility, but he hadn’t shared with them where exactly he was living.</p><p>He at one point lived independently and other times with family. Chamille Sopys said more can be done to protect people who are outside during extreme weather.</p><p>“The facilities that used to be open when I was growing up no longer exist for certain people, and I feel like that is a horrible situation especially for a lot of the people who are homeless and it’s not their complete fault that they’re homeless,” said Chamille Sopys. “They might have learning disabilities or something of that nature to the point where they cannot get jobs and they fall into that stigmatism. Like my uncle, he was one of those people.”</p><p>The family released balloons in his memory this past weekend. Chamille Sopys, who lived with her uncle and grandmother at one point, will remember how her uncle helped her with math homework as a child and for his sense of humor.</p><p>“He was a very family-oriented person,” she said. “When it came to his friends, he would do anything for his friends to the point where we always felt like people took advantage of him.”</p><p>The news of Sopys’ death comes as the area was under another extreme <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/27/weather-storms-heat-wind" target="_blank" ><u>heat </u></a>warning, with the heat index expected to reach 110 to 115 degrees, according to the National Weather Service. Residents in Chicago can call 3-1-1 to request well-being checks for neighbors or loved ones during the heat.<br></p>
